facts.title: Named For Its Colors
facts.text: Chromium gets its name from the Greek word "chroma," meaning color, because so many of its compounds are vividly pigmented. French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin isolated the metal in 1797-1798 from a bright orange-red Siberian mineral called crocoite (lead chromate). He was struck by the rainbow of greens, yellows, reds, and oranges its salts could produce.

facts.title: The Hardest Common Metal
facts.text: Chromium is the hardest pure metal known, scoring about 8.5 on the Mohs scale, harder than hardened steel and nearly as hard as topaz. This extreme hardness, combined with a high melting point of 1907 degrees Celsius, is why it is used to harden alloys and create wear-resistant coatings. Despite being so hard, pure chromium is also quite brittle at room temperature.

facts.title: The Reason Steel Doesn't Rust
facts.text: Stainless steel is defined as steel containing at least 10.5 percent chromium, and the chromium is what makes it "stainless." The metal reacts with oxygen to form an ultra-thin, invisible, self-repairing passive layer of chromium oxide just a few nanometers thick. If the surface is scratched, this protective film instantly reforms, sealing the metal against corrosion.

facts.title: Rubies And Emeralds Owe It Their Color
facts.text: The deep red of a ruby and the lush green of an emerald both come from trace amounts of chromium ions replacing aluminum in the crystal. The same chromium impurity produces red in one gem and green in the other because the surrounding crystal structure changes how the ion absorbs light. Chromium-doped synthetic ruby also powered the very first working laser, built by Theodore Maiman in 1960.

facts.title: A Metal Magnetic Only When Cold
facts.text: Pure chromium is the only elemental solid that is antiferromagnetic at room temperature, meaning its atomic magnetic moments line up in alternating opposite directions and cancel out. It loses this ordered magnetism above its Neel temperature of about 38 degrees Celsius, becoming an ordinary paramagnet. This unusual behavior makes chromium a favorite subject for physicists studying magnetism.

facts.title: Glittering Shop-Window Chrome
facts.text: The shiny "chrome" finish on car bumpers, motorcycle parts, and bathroom fixtures is a thin layer of chromium applied by electroplating. The coating is prized because it stays bright, resists tarnish and scratches, and reflects light almost like a mirror. Decorative chrome plating boomed in the 1920s and 1930s and became an icon of the automotive age.

facts.title: An Essential Trace Nutrient
facts.text: Your body contains only a few milligrams of chromium, yet the trivalent form, chromium(III), is generally considered a trace nutrient that helps the hormone insulin work efficiently. It is found in foods such as broccoli, whole grains, nuts, and brewer's yeast. The amounts needed are tiny, and chromium(III) should not be confused with its toxic cousin.

facts.title: A Tale Of Two Charges
facts.text: Chromium's most famous oxidation states behave like opposites: chromium(III) is essential and relatively harmless, while chromium(VI), or hexavalent chromium, is a recognized carcinogen. Hexavalent chromium contamination of drinking water is the pollutant made famous by the legal case dramatized in the film Erin Brockovich. Industries that once used it for plating and pigments now face strict regulation worldwide.

facts.title: Forged Inside Dying Stars
facts.text: Chromium is created deep inside massive stars and during supernova explosions through nuclear fusion of lighter elements. Its most abundant isotope, chromium-52, is built up in the same processes that forge iron, one of the most stable nuclei in the universe. Astronomers detect chromium's spectral fingerprints in the Sun and in distant stars, tracing how galaxies enrich themselves with metals.

facts.title: Tanning Leather And Protecting Wood
facts.text: Roughly 90 percent of the world's leather is tanned using chromium(III) salts, a process that takes hours instead of the weeks needed by older vegetable methods. Chromium compounds also serve as wood preservatives, green and yellow pigments, and catalysts in the chemical industry. Most chromium ore is mined as chromite, with South Africa and Kazakhstan holding the largest reserves.
